opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's one of the things I'm most excited about right now, because it brings together two ideas that grew up in separate communities: economics and statistics.

Let me start with the problem. Classical statistics mostly imagines a single decision-maker looking at data. Think about a regulator like the FDA. A pharmaceutical company comes in wanting approval for a drug. The company knows things the regulator doesn't. It has private information about whether the drug is likely to work, and it has its own incentives. If the drug doesn't work, the company still makes money if it gets approved. So this is a principal-agent problem, and the hypothesis test is really one part of a contract between two parties with different information and different interests.

Once you see it that way, you ask: how should I design the statistical protocol so that the agent's incentives line up with the truth? You want the protocol to be incentive-compatible. A company that believes its drug doesn't work shouldn't find it profitable to run the trial at all. That's the screening idea from contract theory: you design a menu of options so that agents reveal their type by what they choose.

This is where e-values come in, and it was a bit of a surprise to us. An e-value is a nonnegative random variable whose expectation under the null is at most one. You can read it as the payoff of a bet against the null. If the null is true, you can't expect to make money by betting against it. That's exactly the kind of condition you need in a contract. If the payoff to the agent is tied to an e-value, then an agent whose product is null, a drug that doesn't work, can't expect to profit. So the incentive constraint and the statistical validity constraint turn out to be essentially the same mathematical object. In our work we showed that, in a precise sense, the incentive-compatible contracts correspond to e-values. That's a satisfying moment, when two theories from different fields click together.

So how does this change how I think about uncertainty quantification? A few ways.

First, uncertainty quantification isn't just a property of a model or a dataset. It lives in a social context. Who's using the uncertainty statement? What are their incentives? What will they do with it? A p-value or confidence interval that's perfectly valid for a single analyst can be gamed when agents choose which experiments to run, when to stop, and what to report. E-values handle optional stopping and continuous monitoring gracefully, and they compose, since you can multiply them across independent studies. Those properties are just what you need when lots of strategic actors interact over time.

Second, it moves us from a purely inferential view to a decision-theoretic and economic one, which I've long argued machine learning needs. We keep building systems as if there's one big intelligence making predictions. Real systems are markets, platforms, and institutions, with many agents, each holding a bit of information and each with their own goals. Uncertainty has to be quantified in a way that survives those interactions.

Third, the betting interpretation is intuitive. Saying "I'm willing to bet at these odds against the null, and here's my accumulated wealth" is something people understand, and it's honest about evidence in a way a lot of p-value rituals aren't. That links to the work by Glenn Shafer and Vladimir Vovk on game-theoretic probability, and to the recent work on anytime-valid inference by Aaditya Ramdas and others. Contract theory adds the piece that says the bet isn't just a metaphor. It can be an actual economic mechanism.

And this connects with conformal prediction and the other distribution-free methods we've been developing. The theme across all of it is that we want guarantees that don't depend on believing a model is correct, and now, guarantees that don't depend on everyone behaving nicely. That's the kind of robustness you need if machine learning is going to sit inside high-stakes institutions like medicine, finance, and regulation.

So for me, the contract-theory view says uncertainty quantification is ultimately about trust between parties. E-values give us a currency for that trust.

r001.rationale: It says the incentive and statistical validity constraints are essentially the same mathematical object and that incentive-compatible contracts correspond to e-values, communicating the requested equivalence.

r002.rationale: It says uncertainty quantification lives in a social context shaped by who uses it and their incentives, and discusses how agents choose experiments, stopping, and reporting.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start by saying that I've never been fully comfortable with the phrase "uncertainty quantification" as it's usually deployed in machine learning. It tends to suggest that uncertainty is a property of the model, something you compute and attach to a prediction like a label. But uncertainty is really a property of a decision situation. Somebody is going to act on this output, that somebody has incentives, and often there are multiple parties whose incentives don't align. So the question I've been pushing on is not "how uncertain is the model" but "how do you design the interaction between a learner and the people who consume its outputs so that the uncertainty gets handled sensibly by everyone involved."

That's where contract theory comes in. In economics, contract theory is about principals and agents. A principal wants something done, an agent has private information or private effort, and you design a mechanism so that the agent's self-interested behavior leads to good outcomes for the principal. Now map that onto statistics. The classical setup is that one person collects data, one person analyzes it, one person decides. In reality those are different people. A drug company runs the trial, a regulator decides on approval. A platform's data scientist builds the model, a downstream team deploys it. The person with the data has incentives that the decision maker doesn't share. So you need a statistical protocol that's robust to that, one that yields valid inferences even when the party generating evidence is strategic.

And e-values turn out to be the natural currency for that. The reason is simple once you see it. A p-value is a snapshot; it's valid at one pre-specified moment and it doesn't compose well. You can't multiply p-values, you can't keep collecting evidence and stop when you like, you can't hand your evidence to someone else who continues the experiment. An e-value is a nonnegative random variable with expectation at most one under the null, and that single property means it behaves like wealth in a betting game. You can multiply e-values across stages, you can stop at any time and the validity is preserved, and when you combine evidence from different agents you simply average or multiply. That's exactly the kind of object you want in a contract. The regulator can say to the pharma company: you do whatever experiments you want, adaptively, strategically, and I will approve if your accumulated e-value crosses a threshold. The agent has every incentive to bet aggressively, but the mathematics guarantees the principal's error rate regardless.

So what this does to my view of uncertainty quantification is that it moves the locus. The guarantee lives in the protocol, in the contract, not in a posterior distribution inside someone's head or inside a model. I'm a Bayesian by training, I love posteriors, but a posterior is a single agent's object. When you have many agents with conflicting interests, there's no shared prior you can appeal to. What you can appeal to is a frequentist-style guarantee that holds no matter what the other side does, and e-values deliver that in a way that's dynamic and compositional.

There's also a deep connection to the game-theoretic foundations of probability that Shafer and Vovk developed, where probability itself is defined through betting. I find that very appealing for engineering systems. If I'm building a marketplace, or a recommendation system, or a system that mediates between many people, I want statistical statements that are enforceable, that someone can be held to. "The posterior probability is 0.93" isn't enforceable. "Under this contract your e-process never exceeds the threshold with probability more than alpha unless the alternative is true" is enforceable.

So I'd summarize it this way: uncertainty quantification shouldn't be about decorating predictions with error bars. It should be about designing the economic and statistical rules of engagement so that collectives of learners and decision makers, each with their own interests, arrive at good outcomes. Contract theory supplies the incentive side, e-values supply the evidential side, and the two fit together more naturally than I initially expected.

r001.rationale: The response connects contract incentives with e-values, but does not state an if-and-only-if correspondence between incentive compatibility and the e-value condition.

r002.rationale: It frames uncertainty as a property of the decision situation and emphasizes that its handling depends on how evidence is gathered and used within the protocol.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the connection encourages us to view uncertainty quantification as part of a decision-making relationship. Someone has information, someone else has to act on that information, and we need to ask what makes the communication credible. That’s very much the language of contract theory: what can you promise, what can be verified, and what incentives does the arrangement create?

An e-value gives you a particularly clean mathematical ingredient. It’s a nonnegative statistic whose expectation is at most one under the null hypothesis. You can interpret it as the payoff from a bet that is fair, or unfavorable, under the null. A large observed payoff is therefore evidence against that null. The expectation constraint is what makes the evidential claim accountable.

There’s an important distinction, though: an e-value isn’t the probability that a hypothesis is wrong, and it doesn’t by itself make a scientist or a data provider truthful. You still need to specify the information available, the permitted actions, and the incentives. But it gives you a useful building block for a statistical contract.

What interests me is that this moves uncertainty beyond simply attaching an error bar to a prediction. We can ask how evidence remains valid as people collect more data, adapt their decisions, and interact. With appropriately constructed sequential e-processes, for example, you can retain guarantees under optional stopping. That’s a step toward uncertainty quantification that fits the way decisions actually unfold.

r001.rationale: The response describes e-values as a building block for statistical contracts, but does not state an if-and-only-if correspondence between incentive compatibility and the e-value condition.

r002.rationale: It ties uncertainty quantification to how evidence is gathered and used, including available information, sequential data collection, adaptive decisions, and interaction.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the connection is useful because it asks us to make uncertainty operational. Rather than simply reporting a confidence level, we ask: what can someone do with this claim, and what protection do they have if the claim is wrong?

An e-value is a nonnegative quantity whose expectation is at most one under the null hypothesis. You can think of it as the payoff from a bet: if the null is true, there’s a constraint on how much that bet can pay on average. A large observed value is evidence against the null, but it isn’t the probability that the null is false.

The contract-theoretic perspective brings in incentives. Suppose one party has information and another party needs to act on it. How do we structure the reporting and the consequences so that the uncertainty statement is credible? The expectation bound gives us a useful mathematical ingredient for that kind of arrangement.

And with an appropriate sequential construction, these guarantees can survive adaptive data collection and stopping. That matters because real decision-making is sequential. You gather information, take an action, and gather more information. So I see this connection as moving uncertainty quantification toward guarantees that remain meaningful when people actually use them.

r001.rationale: The response connects the e-value expectation bound to incentives in contract theory, but does not state an if-and-only-if correspondence between incentive compatibility and the e-value condition.

r002.rationale: It ties the guarantees to how evidence is gathered, explaining that an appropriate sequential construction can handle adaptive data collection and stopping.
